captions.instagram:
How do scissors work?

You have used them since nursery school, and they are cleverer than they look. Open up a pair of scissors in 3D: two levers, two edges that pass without meeting, and blades bent on purpose so they touch at one travelling point. Then find out why they fail in a left hand.

→ A pair of scissors is just three parts: two steel halves and one screw.
→ Each half is a lever, and the pivot screw is its fulcrum.
→ Squeeze with 20 newtons and the blades push with 100 near the pivot, but only 16 at the tip.
→ The two edges never meet: they slide past each other and shear the paper between them.
→ Open a gap wider than the paper and it just folds instead of shearing.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/scissorsclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How do scissors work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
You have used them since nursery school, and they are cleverer than they look. Open up a pair of scissors in 3D: two levers, two edges that pass without meeting, and blades bent on purpose so they touch at one travelling point. Then find out why they fail in a left hand.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/scissorsclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/scissorsclear

In this video:
• Three parts, crossed. A pair of scissors is two steel halves and one pivot screw.
• Two levers, one fulcrum. Each half is a lever that turns about the pivot.
• A shear, not a slice. The two edges never meet.
• One touching point. The blades are slightly bowed and twisted, so they touch only where the edges cross, and that point runs from the pivot to the tip as you cut.
• Why scissors are handed. A closing hand pushes the thumb handle one way and pulls the finger handle the other.
• One idea, many tools. Tailor's shears, pinking shears, tin snips, compound snips and secateurs all use the same lever and the same passing edges, reshaped for the job.
